passages.t: A guarded city with few people in it
passages.happening:
‘When the wall had been rebuilt and I had set the doors in place, the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed’ (verse 1). Nehemiah puts his brother Hanani in charge of Jerusalem, with Hananiah the commander of the fortress, ‘because he was a faithful man who feared God more than most’ (verse 2).

He gives orders for the gates: “Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot” (verse 3). The residents are to stand guard, some at their posts and some in front of their own homes.

‘Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not yet been rebuilt’ (verse 4). ‘Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials, and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The wall is built, but walls do not make a city. Jerusalem needs people, and Nehemiah's next task is to fill it. That task is finished in chapter 11, when one family in ten moves into the city by lot.

Gates were the weakest points of an ancient city. Keeping them shut until the sun was hot, well after dawn, meant that no one could take the city in the early morning. And residents guarding the sections near their own homes is the same practical arrangement as the building of chapter 3.

Notice that gatekeepers, singers and Levites are appointed together. The walled city was also the temple city, where guarding and worship went together.

And notice how Nehemiah describes an administrative decision: ‘Then my God put it into my heart’ (verse 5). He understands ordinary planning as God's prompting.
passages.later: The register Nehemiah found is the same list that stands in Ezra 2, and it opens in the same words: ‘Now these are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar its king’ (Ezra 2:1).
passages.asks: Nehemiah chose a man who feared God more than most to keep the city. Ask what you look for in the people you trust with what matters. And ask what God may have put into your heart to do that looks, from the outside, like ordinary planning.

passages.t: The register of the first return
passages.happening:
Nehemiah copies out the register in full. ‘These are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar its king. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town’ (verse 6).

It lists their leaders, Zerubbabel and Jeshua first (verse 7); the lay families by ancestor and by town (verses 8-38); the priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers (verses 39-45); the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants (verses 46-60); and those who could not prove their descent, among them priests who were kept from the most holy things ‘until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim’ (verse 65).

‘The whole assembly numbered 42,360’ (verse 66), besides servants, singers and animals. The governor, the family heads and the rest of the people give gold, silver and priestly garments for the work (verses 70-72). And they settle in their towns: ‘And by the seventh month the Israelites had settled in their towns’ (verse 73).
passages.hearers:
The list comes from the early days of the return, nearly a century before Nehemiah. It is almost identical to Ezra 2. The first returns probably took place over some years rather than in one caravan, and the register may gather several groups together.

Placed here, the list ties Nehemiah's generation to the first returnees. It answers the question that Ezra 2 answered: who belongs to the restored community? The answer is a people with families and hometowns, named one by one.

Family records mattered deeply after the exile. The community was defined by descent from those who had been carried away, and the priesthood was limited by law to the descendants of Aaron. Those who could not prove their descent were not expelled from the people. The priests among them were kept from the most holy portions until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim, the sacred lots kept by the high priest. The question was left open, not closed harshly.

The governor in verse 65 is called by a Persian title, and the gifts are counted in gold darics, the coin of the Persian kings from Darius I onward, and in minas of silver.

The last verse leads straight into chapter 8, which begins in the seventh month, much as the list in Ezra 2 leads into the gathering of Ezra 3.
passages.later: The list in Ezra 2 ends with the same verse that ends this one, and the next chapter opens in the same month: ‘By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem’ (Ezra 3:1).
passages.hard:
Why do the numbers in this list differ from the list in Ezra 2?

The two lists are clearly the same document, and both give a total of 42,360. But many of the family figures differ slightly, a few names are spelled differently, and the separate figures add up to less than the total in both lists: about 31,089 here and 29,818 in Ezra.

Interpreters explain this in several ways. Some think the two books keep copies of the register made at different stages, one perhaps of those who planned to go and the other of those who arrived, or with later updates. Others point to the known difficulty of copying numbers accurately in ancient manuscripts, where numerals and number words are easily confused. And the gap between the parts and the total may mean that the total counts people, such as women, who are not listed by family.

None of these explanations is certain. What is clear is that the writers did not try to smooth the differences away, and that the list's purpose, to show who belonged to the restored community, is not affected by them.
passages.asks: Nehemiah went back to the beginning and read the names of those who first came home. Ask whose faithfulness you are standing on. And ask how you might remember them by name, as this list does.
